Acne is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by follicular inflammation and keratinization abnormalities, commonly seen in adolescence and often occurring on the face, neck, chest, and back.

Treatment typically involves avoiding contact with sensitizing substances and using topical corticosteroids and other medications. It is recommended to seek medical attention promptly to avoid exacerbating the condition.

Basal cell carcinoma is the most common type of skin cancer, usually occurring on the head, neck, and upper limbs, presenting with symptoms such as red patches, ulcers, and crust formation. A definitive diagnosis would require a tissue biopsy.

Basal cell carcinoma is a common type of skin malignancy that usually grows slowly, but if left untreated, it may invade surrounding tissues. It is recommended for the patient to seek medical attention promptly for further treatment.

This is a photo of the hand showing multiple purple-red papules on the extensor side of the finger joints, some of which are merging into plaques with scales on the surface, typical of dermatomyositis. Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune disease characterized by chronic inflammation of the skin and muscles. It usually requires skin biopsy, blood tests for diagnosis, and may necessitate long-term immunosuppressive therapy.

This is a photo of the lower limbs showing scattered erythematous papules, consistent with a diagnosis of drug eruption. Drug eruption refers to skin lesions caused by medications, typically presenting with rash, itching, erythema, and other symptoms. The key to treating drug eruption is to immediately discontinue the offending medication and provide appropriate anti-allergic treatment based on the symptoms.

This patient presents with diffuse distribution of pinhead-sized red papules and plaques on the trunk and upper limbs, which have coalesced into large patches, consistent with the features of erythema multiforme. Erythema multiforme is a common skin condition often caused by infections, drug reactions, or other factors, characterized by rash and patches, typically accompanied by itching or burning sensation.

The scalp shows clustered nodules with hair loss on the surface, clinically consistent with folliculitis decalvans. This condition is a chronic inflammatory disease commonly seen on the scalp, which can result in follicle damage and permanent hair loss.

This is a photo of the hands showing dark red annular lesions on the dorsum of both hands, some of which have merged into a map-like pattern with raised edges, consistent with the clinical presentation of granuloma annulare. Granuloma annulare is a common skin condition characterized by nodular or papular plaques on the skin, often found on the hands, feet, or head. The exact cause of granuloma annulare is unknown, but it may be associated with allergic reactions, infections, or autoimmune factors. Treatment options may include topical corticosteroids or cryotherapy. It is recommended to consult a dermatologist for further evaluation and management.

This is a photo of the trunk showing large areas of erythematous macules with moisture, erosion, and crust in skin folds, consistent with the diagnosis of familial benign chronic pemphigus. Pemphigus is a rare autoimmune disease characterized by blisters, erosion, and ulcers on the skin and mucous membranes, usually with a chronic progressive course. Treatment often involves oral corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and topical anti-inflammatory medications. Patients require regular follow-ups and close monitoring of disease progression.

Xanthoma disseminatum is a common skin condition that typically occurs in children and adolescents. It is characterized by the presence of pale yellow papules or plaques on the skin, which are smooth to touch and commonly seen on the face, neck, and trunk. The exact cause of this condition is not well understood, although it may be related to abnormalities in lipid metabolism. Xanthoma disseminatum is usually benign and does not lead to other serious health issues. Treatment mainly involves observation and moisturizing care.

Based on the description and appearance of the red papules and plaques on the back of the neck with smooth and shiny surface and irregular shape in the photo, the diagnosis of keloid is made. Keloid is a common skin condition characterized by overgrowth of collagen at the site of a healed skin injury, often accompanied by itching or pain. Treatment options include topical medications, laser therapy, among others, and the specific treatment plan should be tailored based on the severity of the condition and individual differences.

Based on the description of the lesion, the patient has a circular red patch with central regression and raised nodules at the edges under the right outer canthus. The differential diagnoses include sarcoidosis and granuloma annulare. Sarcoidosis is a chronic multi-system disease that can cause tissue proliferation and nodules, commonly affecting the eyes, skin, and other areas. Granuloma annulare, on the other hand, is an inflammatory skin condition characterized by localized redness, swelling, and raised edges. To confirm the diagnosis, it is recommended for the patient to seek medical attention promptly for further evaluation and diagnosis.

The case presents as oval-shaped red patches with thick yellow adherent scales. Considering the clinical presentation and pathological features, the diagnosis of cutaneous lupus erythematosus is likely. Cutaneous lupus erythematosus is a subtype of lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease that primarily affects the skin, manifesting as red patches, scales, rashes, and other symptoms. Treatment typically involves the use of corticosteroids and immunosuppressants.

In this photo, large areas of edematous erythema and local capillary dilation are visible on the cheeks, consistent with the clinical presentation of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. A comprehensive diagnosis should be made based on the patient's medical history, laboratory tests, and other clinical features.

This is a photo of the toe cleft, showing localized skin staining, keratosis, and desquamation. These symptoms are not directly associated with Lyme disease. Possible diagnoses could include fungal infection, eczema, or skin issues caused by dryness. Further evaluation is recommended to confirm the diagnosis.

In this patient, there are round erythematous patches in front of the ear with uniform color and well-defined margins, suggestive of a melanocytic nevus. Melanocytic nevi are common skin lesions characterized by an overgrowth of melanocytes, which can be congenital or acquired. Most melanocytic nevi are benign but should still be monitored for any changes and regularly evaluated. Treatment options include laser therapy or surgical excision if the nevus causes cosmetic concerns. Maintaining good skin protection and regular skin examinations are also crucial.

Melanoma is a malignant tumor that typically originates from melanocytes in the skin. It can occur in any part of the body, including the upper limbs. Melanoma often presents as irregular dark brown or black patches, sometimes with features like uneven colors and irregular borders. Early diagnosis and treatment of melanoma are crucial, as timely surgical excision and other treatments can improve patient survival rates and prognosis.

This is an image showing skin lesions on the anterior chest, with large raised red patches and nodules, possibly accompanied by desquamation, clinically suspected to be a fungal infection. Further evaluation with fungal culture or skin scraping may be needed to confirm the diagnosis.

In a patient presenting with purple patches on the trunk with red raised edges, this may be a symptom of purpura. Purpura is a hemorrhagic disease commonly seen on the skin and mucous membranes, characterized by purple patches, ecchymosis, or petechiae, often with raised red edges. To confirm the diagnosis, it is necessary to combine the patient's medical history and perform further auxiliary examinations, such as skin biopsy.

The photo shows large purplish-red patches on the lateral aspect of the calf, with scattered ulcers and brownish-yellow depressions in the center, which are characteristic features of progressive lipoid necrobiosis. Progressive lipoid necrobiosis is a rare skin condition, typically caused by local skin ischemic necrosis due to vascular diseases, clinically presenting with purplish-red patches, ulcers, and depressions. Treatment involves addressing the underlying cause and closely monitoring the progression of the disease.

Patients present with purplish-red papules, smooth surface, merging together, and some arranged in a linear pattern, consistent with a diagnosis of filariasis. Filariasis is a disease caused by nematodes parasitizing in the subcutaneous tissues of the human body, commonly caused by filarial worms such as Wuchereria bancrofti. The diagnosis of filariasis requires a combination of clinical symptoms, skin manifestations, and necessary laboratory tests.

Neutrophilic dermatosis is a rare chronic disease characterized by the presence of purple-red nodules or patches on the skin, which are caused by the deposition of neutrophils in the skin tissue. This condition may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, etc. Treatment typically involves the use of corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and other medications. Timely diagnosis and treatment are crucial for controlling the progression of the disease.

In the genital area, there are red papules with blood crusts, indicating a possible pubic lice infection. Pubic lice, caused by parasitic insects, is a sexually transmitted disease with symptoms such as itching, redness, bleeding points, and visible nits in the pubic area. It is recommended that the patient seek medical attention promptly for diagnosis and treatment to prevent worsening of the condition and transmission to others.

The photo shows multiple oval dark red patches with collarette scales, which are typical manifestations of pityriasis rosea. Pityriasis rosea is a chronic and recurrent skin condition characterized by red patches and scales, commonly seen in middle-aged and elderly individuals, especially women. The exact cause is unclear but may be related to factors such as genetics and immunity. Treatment typically involves topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, etc. Regular follow-up and avoidance of triggering factors are crucial for disease control.

Majocchi's granuloma is a common skin condition characterized by diffuse erythematous patches with bran-like scaling. It may be associated with fungal infection or allergic reactions and commonly affects the scalp, trunk, and extremities. Treatment typically involves topical antifungal and anti-inflammatory medications, along with avoiding humid environments and irritants.

Hidradenitis suppurativa is a common skin condition characterized by well-defined, raised, hyperkeratotic lesions with central atrophy. This condition can cause rough, dry skin with occasional itching. Treatment usually involves the use of keratolytic agents, topical medications, or phototherapy to improve symptoms.

In this case, the diffuse erythema on the top of the head with patchy scratching may indicate a contact dermatitis caused by artificial factors. Contact dermatitis is a type of skin inflammation that is often triggered by exposure to irritant substances such as chemicals, allergens, or pathogens. It is advisable to seek medical attention promptly for proper diagnosis and treatment.

On this photo, deep red nodules with partial skin breakdown and bleeding, forming scabs, can be seen on the extensor aspect of the upper limb. This is a typical presentation of nodular prurigo. Nodular prurigo is a chronic relapsing skin condition characterized by nodular lesions on the skin, accompanied by itching sensation triggered by scratching. Treatment options include the use of topical corticosteroids or oral antihistamines to alleviate symptoms, and avoiding scratching to prevent infection.

The description of oval-shaped red patches covered with thick white scales is consistent with the clinical presentation of psoriasis. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by excessive keratinocyte proliferation, presenting with red patches, scales, and itching. In addition to clinical features, the diagnosis of psoriasis can be confirmed through methods such as skin biopsy.

On this photo of the face, we can see scattered red papules with irregular shapes and partial fusion, which are characteristic of nodular disease. These findings, combined with clinical symptoms and signs, support the diagnosis of nodular disease. Nodular disease is a chronic non-caseating inflammatory condition that can affect various organs in the body, commonly found in lymph nodes, lungs, eyes, and skin. Treatment usually involves monitoring, medication, and sometimes surgical intervention when necessary.

This is a picture showing several light red infiltrative nodules on the skin of the penis with clear borders, consistent with the clinical presentation of scabies. Scabies is an infectious disease caused by the scabies mite, often presenting with skin rash and itching, commonly seen in skin folds and areas of skin-to-skin contact. It is recommended to seek medical attention promptly for diagnosis and treatment.

This is a photo of hands showing ivory-colored atrophy of the fingertips skin and thinning of the fingers, indicative of scleroderma. Scleroderma is an autoimmune disease characterized by fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, resulting in skin hardening, stiffness, and impaired joint mobility, significantly impacting the patient's quality of life and function. Treatment mainly focuses on symptom control, pain and inflammation relief, and organ function preservation.

The red patches, papules, and small pustules appearing on the forehead and nose may indicate seborrheic dermatitis or rosacea. Seborrheic dermatitis is a common skin inflammation that often occurs in the T-zone (forehead, nose, and chin), characterized by excessive sebum production leading to oily skin, blackheads, and inflammation. On the other hand, rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin condition, presenting as facial redness, papules, and pustules, which can be easily confused and misdiagnosed. It is recommended to consult a dermatologist for an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.

Facial black papules may be caused by seborrheic keratosis or melanocytic nevi, further investigation is needed for a definitive diagnosis. Seborrheic keratosis is a common skin condition characterized by oily papules on the face or other parts of the body, often accompanied by itching or inflammation. Melanocytic nevi, on the other hand, are pigmented patches on the skin, mostly benign, but it is important to monitor for signs of malignancy.

Based on the description of the lesion in the photo and the patient's medical history, the initial diagnosis is squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma is a common malignant skin tumor that typically originates from squamous cells in the epidermis and can occur on areas such as the head and neck. Confirmation of the diagnosis requires further tissue biopsy and pathological examination.

In this photo of the upper limb, there is a flat lesion with a dark red color, rough surface, and thin layer of scales, which are consistent with the clinical presentation of in situ squamous cell carcinoma. In situ squamous cell carcinoma is a non-invasive epidermal cancer that typically occurs in sun-exposed areas of the skin, presenting early symptoms as localized skin lesions. Treatment usually involves surgical excision, cryotherapy, or local radiation therapy.

This patient presents with scattered erythematous macules with erosion and crusting, indicative of severe erythema multiforme drug eruption. This condition is typically a severe cutaneous reaction caused by drug hypersensitivity and requires prompt cessation of the offending medication and appropriate management.

This is a photo showing skin lesions on the face, with large patches of erythema on the forehead, bilateral cheeks, and upper lip. Further evaluation is recommended for an accurate diagnosis and treatment plan.

On this photo, there are brownish papules present on the nose, which, combined with the medical history and clinical presentation, are consistent with the features of tuberous sclerosis. Tuberous sclerosis is a rare genetic disorder characterized by the development of multiple benign tumors, skin patches, and neurological issues. This condition typically affects multiple organ systems and requires comprehensive treatment and management.

This is a common allergic skin condition that typically presents with red, itchy wheals and patches of redness, sometimes accompanied by swelling and a burning sensation. Urticaria can be acute, lasting for hours to days, or chronic, lasting for weeks to months. Common triggers include foods, medications, infections, and environmental factors. Treatment for urticaria may involve avoiding allergens, taking oral or topical corticosteroids, antihistamines, etc.

The patient presents with dark red patches and rough scales on the forearm. Possible diagnoses considered include chronic eczema, psoriasis, and common warts. A skin microscopy examination is recommended for a definitive diagnosis.

This is a photo showing irregular depigmented patches with clear boundaries on the back of the hand joints, consistent with the presentation of vitiligo. Vitiligo is a chronic autoimmune skin condition characterized by localized depigmented patches on the skin, often accompanied by hair discoloration. The etiology is complex, involving factors such as genetics and autoimmunity. Treatment options include topical corticosteroids, phototherapy, systemic immunomodulators, and patients should avoid sun exposure, irritating medications, and cosmetics.

This is a photo of the perineal area showing dark red patches in the groin area with clear borders, which is a typical presentation of Lyme disease. The brown irregular oval-shaped papules you described may be indicative of melanoma, a malignant skin tumor that usually presents as dark brown or black with irregular borders and large diameter. Diagnosing melanoma typically requires skin examination and pathological tests to confirm the diagnosis and determine the treatment plan.

Sebaceous cysts are common skin lesions that typically occur when a hair follicle is blocked, leading to the accumulation of sebum and forming a cyst. Treatment options include topical antibiotic creams or surgical excision.

Bullous pemphigoid is a chronic, autoimmune skin disease characterized by scattered blisters and tense bullae on the skin surface, often accompanied by itching and pain. The etiology may be related to abnormal activation of the immune system, genetic factors, etc. Treatment typically includes corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, local care, and avoiding triggering factors. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for controlling the progression of the condition.

Grey-black papules with a dark center are consistent with the features of a melanocytic nevus. Melanocytic nevi are common skin lesions typically caused by the deposition of melanin in skin cells. Further investigations such as dermatoscopy or biopsy are recommended to confirm the diagnosis.

Photocontact dermatitis is a skin inflammation caused by prolonged exposure to ultraviolet light, commonly seen on exposed areas such as hands and neck. Treatment usually involves avoiding direct sunlight and using topical corticosteroid creams. It is recommended to seek medical attention promptly for a professional diagnosis and treatment.

This is a photo showing pale red infiltrative patches on the face with unclear borders and no obvious scales, indicative of sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is a chronic non-caseating inflammatory disease that primarily affects the lungs and lymphatic tissues but can also involve other organs such as the skin. This is a photo of a finger showing two water blisters with clear fluid. Combined with the symptoms appearing after sun exposure, the preliminary diagnosis is likely to be solar dermatitis.
